info.title: The Complete OpenSuSE Mail Server
info.subtitle: ... or how to really understand a full IMAP/SMTP/HTTPS/Webmail setup

sect1.title: Introduction
sect1.para: With the almost ubiquitous presence of mobile devices it becomes crucial to be able to access mail from any device anywhere and still read and manipulate the same mails regardless of which device is used. The easiest way to achieve this with close to zero setup effort is to use a public mail provider, for example GMail, Hotmail etc.

However for users that require more fine grained control over message handling a public mail provider might not be a viable option. Reasons that might require such a setup includes but are not limited to:

listitem.para: need for automatic processing of messages with external programs at message arrival (such as automatic replies depending on message content or perform other pre-defined actions such as scannig messages for viruses)
control over mail backup
collection of mails from several accounts into one master repository
unable to comply with the license of the public mail provider
need for an ad-free mail client
needs mail to be sent from a specific domain
privacy concerns

sect1.para: The rest of this tutorial will be spent going through, in details, how to make such a setup based on a OpenSuSE Linux/GNU distribution.

sect2.title: Why another mail tutorial?
sect2.para: There is no shortage of various notes and tutorials trying to show how to do a server setup like this. Our experience is however that many of them, while working (in some respect), have one or more misunderstandings or present obsoleted knowledge based on old ways of doing things. In many cases recommendations are handed down from older tutorial and seen as truth - because they work - but are incomplete or in worst case have been deprecated since long.

This tutorial, while substantially longer, aims at describing a correct and modern setup as well as how it works and how the components interact. Many misunderstanding stem from a poor grasp of the overall picture on how these component fits together. It is our belief that in order to configure a working setup one must understand what one is doing. Just taking random bits of code from "the net" might give, by sheer luck, a working setup but it might as likely have created an open relay for spammers to use (which is very bad).

Especially the SSL/TLS setup using openssl will be covered and explained in more details than usual in descriptions like this since much information available on "the net" is just plain wrong or at best shows very, very, antiquated ways of configuring a SSL/TLS setup.

The setup we will describe in this tutorial will allow any device capable of IMAP message handling (all modern devices do) to connect and synchronize mails from a central repository meaning that any change from any device will be visible to all other devices. The setup will also allow clients to send mails through this server (acting as an SMTPD server).

The setup assumes a "home server" which is not directly connected to the internet and configured as an official mail server for some domain. This also implies the need to relay mails to be sent through a “real” mail server (most likely an ISPs server) that is properly connected to the internet. An overview of the principle of our setup and all constituting parts are shown in .

The goal of this tutorial is therefore to describe, in a very detailed way, how to setup an OpenSuSE server to both act as an IMAP and SMTP server. In addition it will use encrypted communication using a SSL/TLS setup based on the openssl library. This will allow secure mail access from any device (e.g. SmartPhones, Ipads, laptops etc.) using either the device's built-in mail client or optionally connected to our web based mail client.

sect2.title: Applicable OpenSuSE versions and pre-requisites
sect2.para: Much of the information here is generic and not specific to OpenSuSE. However, location and structure of specific configuration files are distribution dependent. This document has been verified on OpenSuSE 11.4 as well as 12.1. Most ofthe details given in this tutorial should also be valid on older 11.x OpenSuSE releases. OpenSuSE resembles the RedHat distribution in some respect but has enough differences of its own to not make it directly compatible. Other systems (for example Ubuntu) uses a rather different setup structure so while the principles still apply the details will not match.

One main difference noticeable between 11.4 and 12.1 is that in 12.1 the older SySV init file handling has been replaced with the more modern systemd init file handling. This has several advantages such as parallelizing startup scripts (hence reducing boot time). Fortunately there is a compatibility layer so that old /etc/init.d/ startup scripts will work as usual and redirect the start/stop commands to systemd (see systemd – boot faster and cleaner)

sect3.title: Installed components
sect3.para: We will assume that all the components listed below are installed on the server. They are all available (with one exception as noted below) from the standard OpenSuSE repository as packages. For now it is enought if these components are installed but not configures - this is what the rest of this tutorial is all about. All these components can be installed from the Yast2 package manager as listed below (the "core packages" indicates the minimum needed packages.)

listitem.para: Apache v2.x - HTTP server (will be referred to as only Apache in the rest of the document).
Core packages: apache2, apache2-prefork, apache2-utils, libapr-util1, libapr1
PHP5 - With at least the modules php5-curl, php5-openssl and php5-sockets installed
Core packages: apache2-mod_php5, php5-mysql,php5-curl, php5-openssl, php5-sockets
Postfix - Mail daemon used to receive and send mails.

para.emphasis: Note: The default mail daemon (MTA) in OpenSuSE 12.1 has changed to exim if a full KDE/X-Windows installation is done. This means installing postfix might trigger a warning that it conflicts with exim and that it will be un-installed. Just answer yes in that case. In case you install the default text server postfix will already have been installed.

listitem.para: Core packages: postfix
Fetchmail - Used to fetch messages from other mail accounts
Core packages: fetchmail
Dovecot v2.x - IMAP server that allows access to your stored mails.

Note: Makes sure that Dovecot 2.x is installed and not Dovecot 1.x. OpenSuSE by default installs the older version 1.x of Dovecot. Dovecot 2.x is available in the OpenSuSE repositories (as dovecot2). We will simple refer to this as Dovecot.
Core packages: dovecot20
MySQL - Database server (needed for the Roundcube webmailer)
Core packages: mysql-community-server, mysql-community-server-client

Procmail - Used for rule based mail filtering which will allow things like sorting mails into folders depending on there content or do other types of automatic processing based on the content of the messages.
Core packages: procmail
Spamassassin - Tool to help identify junk mails (spam)
Core packages: spamassassin, perl-Mail-Spamassassin
openssl - Tool to handle encryption and creation of certificates (this package is installed by default in the Minimal Server Selection)
Core packages: openssl

caution.para: Please make absolutely sure that all of the above components are installed before proceeding!
All necessary component can be installed by running the following command as root
caution.screen: $> zypper in apache2 apache2-prefork apache2-mod_php5 php5-curl \ php5-openssl php5-sockets postfix fetchmail dovecot20 procmail \ mysql-community-server mysql-community-server-client \ spamassassin perl-Mail-Spamassassin

sect3.para: There is also one final package that strictly speaking is not necessary but that we strongly recommend. This is to install a Web-based mail client. Having a web-based mail setup has the advantage that it will allow safe and secure access (using https://) to mails from any networked computer in the world. In this tutorial we will use "Roundcube" (http://roundcube.net/).

The application style of the modern (and AJAX based) Roundcube also makes it a compelling alternative even to native mail clients such as KMail. Roundcube is not as of this writing available as a package for OpenSuSE. However as a Web-applications it is straightforward to install and set it up using the included installer.

sect3.title: What level of experience is needed and how long will it take?
sect3.para: A certain maturity with Linux is assumed but mostly the ability (and willingness) to lookout for details is what matters. As in a mathematical proof every single detail counts. There are literally hundreds of pages in the manuals for all the components we touch upon here so the details described here are only the details that really matters - the need to know details.

Setting up a complete IMAP/SMTP server correctly the first time requires an eye for details. Even experienced administrators will make mistakes. The main advantage with experience is that debugging various issues gets faster since likely problem spots are known by experience.

The setup of a working server will likely take several hours rather than minutes. So patience is needed as well as careful reading with a willingness to go back and double check everything at least three times!

tip.para: We strongly encourage to install the server in a virtual machine installation (for example using VirtualBox) since that will easily allow going back to a known pristine state in case of "unrecoverable error". Compare this with having to re-install a physical server since one is not sure after a while which of all the settings that were changed was wrong.

Once a working server in a virtual machine is established it is also easy to move the virtual server, for example to a new server when the hardware is upgraded. This allows an easy upgrade path to future OpenSuSE version as well without having to reconfigure a complete mail server at each upgrade. When in the future OpenSuSE v13.1, v14.1, etc. comes out there is nothing that prevents running a virtual mail server based on 11.4 or 12.1. The core protocols of the internet are not very likely to have changed dramatically even by then so the virtual server will still be valid.
OpenSuSE has pre-built packages for VirtualBox which makes it straight forward to install.

The only minimal drawback with a virtual server is the need to reserver some RAM memory. However, given that it is perfectly fine to run a complete mail setup on 512MB (or less) this should be considered a small price to pay for the flexibility it will give.

sect2.title: About this document
sect2.para: This tutorial was written in plain text format (UTF-8 encoding) using the DocBook XML markup. To render the styled output from the XML sources the DocBook 1.76.1 XSL stylesheets was used together with the xsltproc XSLT processor

To produce the PDF output the DocBook XML were first transformed into an FO format which was then rendered with the Apache FOP processor into the final PDF format. In order to get the current look and feel of the document a customized XSL stylesheet was used. To style the HTML output both a custom HTML XSL stylesheet and a CSS stylesheet was used.
As source editor oXygen XML editor was used and the transform process into HTML and PDF was controlled by a Phing script.

sect3.title: References for technologies used to produce this document

listitem.para: DocBook, is a defined XML schema that identifies the meaning of different parts of a document. It is specifically well suited to write technical computer related documents but can also be used to write generic documents. By itself DocBook does not care about how the document is displayed (in contrast to for example OpenOffice or Word).

In order to transform the DocBook XML document into something suitable for human reading (such as HTML and PDF) a set of XSL stylesheets are used. They are known as the DocBook XSL stylesheets. The current version as of this writing was 1.76.1
XSL, stands for Extensible Stylesheet Language Family is an overall term for three technologies used to process XML documents into other XML documents. The included technologies are:
XSLT, is a programming language for transforming XML documents into other well formed XML document, for example (X)HTML documents.
XPath, a way to uniquely identify different parts of a well formed XML document. This is used as the search language in the stylesheet to specify what elements to transform.
XSL-FO, is a defined XML schema that defines how a printed output should be displayed. This format can later be easily transformed into other formats suitable for printed output such as PDF or RTF.

xsltproc, is the GNOME projects XSLT processor that uses an XSL(T) program to transform one XML document into another. This is one of the few XSLT processors written in C (most others are written in Java)
fop, is the Apache projects XSL-FO processor. This is primarily used to transform a XSL-FO document into a PDF document.
Oxygen, the XML editor used to for writing the source XML document.

sect1.title: Overview of the components
sect1.para: Unfortunately there isn't one simple program that will do all what we need. Instead we will need a number of components to achieve our goal. A server setup with IMAP/SMTP has some reputation of being “black-magic” to setup. However, this is mostly based on the fact that there are many different parts involved and misunderstanding the role of (or interactions between) the different actors will definitely make the process seem like black magic. So lets start by discussing the parts involved and give a high level logical overview on how the parts interact. For a pictorial overview please refer to

sect2.title: Postfix
sect2.para: This is the SMTP/SMTPD server/daemon that handles the mail protocols we will be using. The Postfix server is abstractly known as an MTA (Mail Transfer Agent) in mail lingo. These are the backbones of message transfer over the internet. The role of the MTAs are to receive and forward messages to other MTAs depending on the end address. This forwarding continues until the message reaches the server that is responsible for the domain the message is addressed to. Once the message is at its final destination it gets delivered to the appropriate user in that domain.
The headers in a typical message will show which MTAs have been passed in the process of delivering the mail from the sender to the recipient.

Initially a user creates a message with some mail client, a mail client is abstractly known as MUA, Mail User Agent) examples are (for example) KMail, Thunderbird or Roundcube. The MUA initially connects to a specified MTA that receives the message. The MTA examines the headers in the mail and determines if it should forward the message to some other MTA or if the message is to be locally delivered.
The reason for using this abstract language instead of referring to the specific programs we are using is to be able to discuss mails without referring to specific protocols or applications.

All of the above is relevant only to officially registered mail servers for a specific domain. These mail serves are recognized in the DNS system with a so called MX record (Mail eXchange). A home based server is normally not an officially recognized mail server fresponsible for a particular domain. Instead the home MTA has to be configured to relay messages it receives from a mail client on to an official mail server. This is normally the mail server at the ISP.

note.para: For a proper email server connected to the internet with a MX (Mail eXchange) record in its DNS entry there are many more details to take into account. For example DKIM, FBL and SPF just to name a few techniques and methods a sysadmin has to be familiar with. Luckily for a home server we can ignore this.

sect2.para: Postfix has two separate and distinct roles, one as a sending server, an SMTP server, and one as a receiving daemon, the SMTPD server. The SMTP server is responsible for sending mail to other servers while the receiving server is a daemon that waits for connections from other servers (or clients) to receive messages. Any messages that should be delivered locally will be stored the users mailbox and any message with a recipient outside the domain the server is responsible for will be forwarded to the next mail server depending on the end address.

By default the assigned port that the receiving MTA server listens on for non-encrypted messages are on port 25, see figure . This is the port that is used both when other MTAs to talk to our server to forward messages as well as the port that mail clients connects on to initially send messages created by the client. (This is how most setups work in practice for historical reasons. However, this is not really in compliance with the original RFCs. In the original specifications port 25 should only be used for MTA to MTA communication and port 587 should be used when a mail clients want to send a new message to a MTA.)

An important part of this setup is that the server will relay all incoming mails to the ISPs mail server which will then send it to the rest of the world. Most ISP will not allow neither outgoing nor incoming traffic on port 25 to any other servers besides their own. This makes it impossible to either directly send messages on port 25 to our server from the ouside or to use any other mail server besides the ISP to forward our messages to. The ISPs block port 25 in an futile attempt to block spams that are sent by Trojan mail servers running on unsuspecting servers. The reason this is futile is that it is as easy to use another port on the server for the spammers. The ISP who is blocking of port 25 is today mainly just an irritation for advanced users. It does not stop spam in any shape or form.

What we need to do in order to send mail via our home server is to use another port, connect to that other port and have postfix relay our message to be sent to our ISPs official mail server. This will of course assume that we have told our SMTPD daemon to listen on that port.
The reasons we do not have our mail clients connect directly to our ISPs mail server but instead going through our home server are twofold:

listitem.para: most ISP does not allow connections to their mail server unless the connections originate from somewhere within their own network. That means it would be impossible to directly connect to the ISP mail server from some device outside the subnet controlled by the ISP, say a smartphone.

the second reason is that we want to be able to send local mails originating in our server (for example system mail) to a valid address (this will also require us to alias a local user to a real email address since most mail servers refuses to pass on messages with a bogus sender address, say "root@localhost")

sect2.title: Dovecot
sect2.para: All messages needs to be stored in a structured way on disk for each user. The two formats mostly used in the Unix/Linux world are.

listitem.para: "maildir" format. This format stores all messages as individual files in a directory structure corresponding to the mail folders defined.

"mbox" format. This format stores all messages lumped together in one file. Historically this is the "original" message storing format. For all practical purposes this should not be usedin new setups.

sect2.para: For all modern installation it is strongly recommended to use the "maildir" format. This is the format we will later on setup Dovecot to use in .

In order to access the mail storage the most flexible way is through an IMAP server (the old and mainly obsolete way being through a POP3 server). It is important to understand that an IMAP server is only responsible to manipulate messages (files) on disk storage. The IMAP server is like mother goose watching over the mail storage. It is not involved in neither sending nor receiving messages in any shape or form. The mail user agent (MUA) connects to the IMAP server and reads the messages for its user. Messages are always kept at the server even after they have been read. This will allow us to later on synchronize the message storage with any other devices and messages that are marked as read on one device will show up read on all other devices as soon as they synchronize their mails. For efficiency reason most mail clients choses to cache messages locally in order not to have to transfer them from the server each time the user decides to open the message.

For now we can also assume that it is the responsibility of some other program to actually store the incoming messages in the mail storage. In mail lingo such a program that stores messages locally on disk is called LDA (Local Delivery Agent).
The main responsibility for an IMAP server is to allow authenticated users to access their messages and update the status of messages such as read or moved ot a different mail folder.
So how can Dovecot keep track of mails if any other program can write new mails into the storage?

On Linux Dovecot uses notifications of file changes to get information on when new mails arrive (using the inotify mechanism). By subscribing to file changes in the mail directories it is possible for dovecot to maintain information and indexes (to quickly find mail). There is also a structure in the maildir directories on where to store new mails so Dovecot knows exactly where to look for new messages.

One reason for choosing Dovecot as our IMAP server (there are others as well) is the fact that it is fast, extremely robust and it is almost impossible to get into a corrupt IMAP state. Even removing all the index files will have no effect. Dovecot will just notice that the files are gone and recreate them by re-reading mails in the storage as necessary.

Dovecot is also the only widely available IMAP server (including some well-known commercially available servers) that fully passes the complete IMAP stress test (see http://www.imapwiki.org/ImapTest/ServerStatus)

note.para: Dovecot is to large extent the creation of a single individual, a finish software engineer with the name of Timo Sirainen.
More information on Dovecot can be found at http://dovecot.org/

sect2.title: Fetchmail
sect2.para: Since external MTA servers can not connect to us directly in order to periodically push new messages to us we must have some method to gather messages from external mail accounts and store them in our mail repository. This is the only way we can receive messages assuming we are configuring a home server which lacks the ability to act as an official domain mail server. Enter here the aptly named program fetchmail.

This program is used to periodically authenticate and fetch new messages from external mail accounts and deliver them locally. We can, for example, setup fetchmail to gather messages from a GMail or Hotmail account so that they can later be accessed by the IMAP server.

The way fetchmail works is that it collects messages from external accounts and then delivers them to our MTA (postfix) on port 25. In effect making it look to postfix like it has received a mail from another MTA, see .
Since fetchmail does not handle authentication at delivery on port 25 postfix must be setup to accept delivery from other daemons that run on the same server without requiring authentication.
Refer to for an illustration where fetchmail fits into the overall setup.

sect2.title: Procmail
sect2.para: The final bit of the puzzle, which strictly speaking is not necessary, will make things like spam filtering and rule based processing of messages possible. Procmail fills the role of a LDA (Local Delivery Agent), the last stage that receives a mail (from postfix) as input before storing it on the file system mail storage.
Procmail configuration is based on rules which uses pattern matching of messages together with a corresponding action to be taken when the pattern matches.

Depending on the user specified rules different actions can be taken depending on the content of the message. A common rule is to store incoming messages in a specific folder based on some criteria. This could for example be used to store identified spams in a specific folder, newsletters in another and the rest of the incoming messages in the inbox. The action in the rules are not just limited to sorting mails in different folders, external programs can also be called when a pattern matches.

The rules that control procmail on how to handle incoming mails are very flexible and it is easy to do things like passing certain mails to some programs for further processing or make automatic replies based on the content in the mail.

Unfortunately the syntax for specifying rules in procmail is an acquired taste at best and takes some getting used to. To ease the writing pain we have collected a few common and useful procmail recipes in .

sect2.title: Roundcube (and Apache)
sect2.para: The above four actors (postfix, dovecot, fetchmail and procmail) are one possible set of applications that can be used to setup a basic mail server. But this can probably be considered one of the standards that both individuals larger organizations use.
In our setup we will also install a Web based mail client that will allow reading and manipulate of messages using any available Web browser.

The mail client will be installed in the same server and talk directly to our IMAP server, i.e. Dovecot. In our setup we will configure Apache (which is our web-server) to allow https:// protocol access to Roundcube.
We have chosen Roundcube since in our opinion it is one of the best free Ajax-based web-mail clients available and is easy to install. A screen shot from Roundcube is shown in

note.para: If you prefer a native client skip this step and use a native mail client (for example KMail in the KDE desktop) as a mail client and configure it to access the local IMAP mail storage.

However we would still recommend you to install Roundcube since it is fairly straight forward and gives universal access to the mail storage from anywhere i the world as long as a browser with intenet connections can be found.

sect2.title: openssl
sect2.para: The openssl library is the de-facto standard encryption library on Linux based systems. It is used to both manipulate and create encryption keys as well as being library for other programs needing to encrypt data. openssl can refer both to the specific command openssl as well as the overall library. The context will determine the usage.

sect2.title: spamassassin
sect2.para: To help identify spam mails (i.e. unwanted junk mail) we will setup and use a Perl library called spamassassin. When a message is about to be delivered to the local user it will first be run through spamassassin. This program will then examine the message based on a number of both pre-defined and heuristic tests and give the mail a score to illustrate the likelihood that the message is junk.

After that it is up to the user that received the mail to determine use the calculated score for further actions. The most common example is to have all messages with a score above X to be stored in the junk mail folder.

sect1.title: The setup process
sect1.para: It is now time to start the setup process. There are a number of steps that needs to be done and as we progress each step will be tested separately as far as possible before we move on to the next and finally the complete system. The steps are explained below and also illustrated in :

listitem.para: Setup Apache to accept https:// traffic by creating a self-signed certificate for Apache. This is necessary so that we can access Roundcube (see below) securely. We start here since this is a self-contained task and can be tested separately.

Setup Dovecot as an IMAP server. We will also configure the server to use a secure connection based on SSL/TLS so we can securely access our mails. This requires us to create another set of self-signed certificates to be used by Dovecot. In addition we will also configure Dovecot to be used as the authentications server for Postfix so that only authenticated users can send mail through our SMTP server (i.e. postfix) this is very important to avoid creating an open relay that could potentially be exploited by a spammer.

Setup Postfix to both accept incoming SMTP traffic (with authentication via Dovecot) as well as sending mail as a relay through to the ISPs SMTP server if the recipient is non-local. We also need to instruct postfix to use procmail as LDA (Local Delivery Agent) to store the mails in a suitable location in the mail storage.
Setup fetchmail to gather mail from any external mail providers and deliver it back to postfix.
Setup spamassassin as a spam filtering engine in the background by using its daemon mode option. Received mails are then run through the spamassassin client (spamc) by procmail.

Setup procmail to use spamassassin to filter spam and store them in a separate folder on the IMAP server. The emails will be delivered to procmail from Postfix (piped) when postfix has decided that the mails should be delivered to a local user. Postfix will invoke procmail to do the local delivery as the user who’s mail we are going to deliver. The instructions to procmail will then be read from <user home directory>/.procmailrc.

Finally we will install and setup Roundcube to access the IMAP server to be able to read and manipulate mails via a Web-interface. This will also include the configuration of a database (MySQL) for Roundcube to make use of.

sect2.title: Some ports and acronyms used
sect2.para: For the TCP/IP communication there are a number of ports and acronyms that are used in a mail setup and it is good to have a shortlist handy. and list the ports and terms we will be using. For historic reasons several port numbers have been used for the same purpose and can lead to some confusion. This is especially true for the port numbers possible to use for secure SMTP. This is further elaborated in the section dealing with procmail setup.
In our setup we will use the secure version of all the protocols involved. This will unfortunately add some steps in the process but doing anything else would be irresponsible!

table.title: Port numbers relating to mail handling

entry.para: Internet Message Access Protocol used to access a mail storage
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol used to speak with a mail server

Simple Mail Transfer Protocol with SSL. Unfortunately this is not an officially recognized/registed port for this purpose. Historically this can be traced back to Appendix A of the 1996 non-standard standard The SSL Protocol Version 3.0 This port should not be used in a modern server setup. Use port 587 (see below) instead.

Email submission (See RFC 2476). This is the officially registered port that should be used when a mail client submits a message to a mail server. The difference with Port 25 is that port 25 should only be used for mail-server to mail-server communication. For historical reason, port 25 has also been used to accept mail client submissions.
Post Office Protocol. The "old" way of accessing a mail storage. Should not be used any more (only listed here for completeness)
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, protocol used to send mail between servers. Note do no confuse with the name of the postfix two daemons SMTP/SMTPD
Internet Message Access Protocol, The protocol between a mail client (e.g. Roundcube) and the mail server. Allows manipulation of mails and synchronizing local mails to a local storage.
Transport Layer Security (formly known as SSL=Secure Socket Layer). There are technical differences but for end users they do behave the same.

There is however one crucial difference in that SSL uses encrypted communication from the very start while TLS uses plain text initially and once the two communicating partners has agreed on encryption the remaining communication is encrypted. This has the advantage that the same port can be used for both encrypted and non encrypted version of a protocol.
Mail Transfer Agent, generic name for the actual program that speaks SMTP (in our case postfix)
Mail User Agent, generic name for the actual mail client (Roundcube in our case)
Local Delivery Agent, generic name for whatever program is responsible for the final mail delivery to the recipients mail box (procmail in our case)

Pluggable Authentication Modules. A generic framework for authentication in a Linux system. This allows clients to perform authentication on a system without knowing the exact methods this authentication is done by. The historic way of performing authentication is by the usage of a user/password file but other ways are available as well, for example via LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) databases.

Simple Authentication and Security Layer. This is another generic framework for authentication but intended to be used by various internet protocols. Usage of this framework allows decoupling of protocol authentication from the actual system it is talking to.
Privacy Enhance Mail, A file format to store SSL/TLS key pairs, commonly used in Unix like systems.

sect2.title: Using SSL/TLS certificates
sect2.para: It is impossible to avoid SSL/TLS (Secure Socket Layer / Transport Layer Security) certificates when configuring a mail server using encrypted communication. We must therefore start with a simplified explanation of key pairs and certificates since they are the heart in the encryption of the data between a client and a server. We will use openssl to manage the so called SSL/TLS encryption (this is used by most people in the Unix world). In . we discuss more in detail how to use this library and associated programs directly to create the necessary keys.

The openssl library supports most (if not all) public used cryptos intended for secure communication and has a very large number of commands and sub-commands. In the following we will only shortly discuss the basic usage of openssl since a full discussion is outside the scope of tis tutorial.

caution.para: openssl has been around for a long time and as it has evolved old parameters which for all practical purposes and intents are deprecated still remains in the program to ensure backward compatibility. This means that the number of commands, options and suboptions possible to give to openssl is mind boggling. Consequently a number of scripts available on "the net" uses old deprecated methods since there are very little incentive to learn new (and better) ways of doing things. The learning curve for openssl is quite steep but luckily we only need a small subset of available commands.

sect3.title: Certificates and keys
sect3.para: In short the SSL/TLS certificates (or SSL/TLS key-pair) serve two purposes:

listitem.para: Form the encryption base for the public key anti-symmetric encryption (different keys for encryption and decryption) used in the SSL/TLS (openssl can also handles symmetric encryption).
Prove the identity of the server that you are connecting to

sect3.para: Public key encryption is based on two different (anti-symmetric) keys, one public key and one private key.

The common way is to use the public key to encrypt data to be sent and the private key to decrypt the same data. However, since the encryption is anti-symmetric it can also be used the other way around. Encrypting with the private key and decrypted with the public key. This can be used to assure that a message comes from a trusted sender as follows.

Assuming we know with 100% certainty that the public key we have really comes from a specific server. If the server then encrypts a message string with its own private key we can decrypt it with the public key and if it decrypts correctly to a valid message we can be reasonable sure that the message really comes from that specific server.

note.para: When talking about SSL/TLS certificates one should really refer to them as X.509 certificates which was standardized a long time ago by ITU-T. The original designer of SSL/TLS certificate handling, Netscape (anyone remembers them?), used the already existing standard of X.509 certificates when they created the SSL/TLS protocol. The use of X.509/SSL/TLS certificates on the internet is described in RFC 5280. The name SSL/TLS certificates has stuck (probably since it is easier to say than X.509) and we will be using this name in this text. However when using openssl to create certificates one specifies X.509 as the format for the certificates so it might be good to know and understand where this strange name comes from.

sect3.para: The public key is in this context is usually referred to as a certificate and is by convention often stored in a file with the ending “*.crt” and the private key (again by convention) is stored in a file with the ending “*.key”. This naming convention is unfortunate since the keys are actually stored in a format known as PEM (see the fact box below).

note.para: The most common format in the Unix world to store the certificates in is in the so called PEM (originally from Privacy Enhanced Mail) format. This is basically a base64 encoding of the binary data that makes up the key (the X.509 specifies the binary format to be in ASN.1). The base64 encoding makes it possible to treat the file as ordinary text files. There are other possible binary formats of keys (and certificates) Windows usually use one of those but we will not discuss this further here.
A common practice to differentiate the contents of the files where the public and private keys are stored is to use different suffixes on the certificate and the private key files.

Even though the keys are in the same format (PEM) they are stored in files with different suffixes. One very common way is to give the public key the ending “*.crt” and the private key the ending “*.key”. This is not ideal since our view is that the file suffix should indicate the technical format/encoding of the file. However, this is common practice so we just accept this for now. (In we show another naming standard that makes more sense to us.)

It is also possible to store both the public and private key in the same file. This is useful for applications where we are never expected to manually hand out a public key but where this is done programmatically between programs/system. The advantage of storing both the public and private key in the same file is obvious; one never risks of mixing the public/private key with the wrong other key.
The PEM format specifies a textual header before the private and public key so they are easily identified even if they are stored in the same file.

sect3.para: In order to prove the authenticity of a public key some company that are trusted (a certification agency, CA) will first encrypt the servers’ public key (against a quite hefty fee). When the public key is distributed it can be verified by the client by decrypting it with the CAs public key. The public key from the CA has to have been previously distributed in some other way so that the client has access to that public key in safe way. Therefore such a public key, which is usually a root certificate, is included with the distribution of browsers. The principle of this is shown in Figure .

Certificates can also be chained. A super trusted company can sign a certificate from a trusted company which in turn could sign your certificate (an intermediate agent). If your browser have the (root) certificate from the super trusted company it will implicitly also validate any child certificates stemming from this super trusted company.

In our setup we will become our own certification agency and create a “super” key pair that we will use to sign (encrypt) the public keys we will be using. Hence the name self-signed certificates. (Technically speaking this is only one definition of the term self-signed certificate and is theoretically not quite correct. It is however a common “miss-use” of this term. In Appendix XX we elaborate on this.)

sect3.title: Protocols using encryption in our setup
sect3.para: In our setup we will use SSL/TLS certificates (encryption) to handle the following protocols

listitem.para: HTTPS - Encrypted communication to our Web-server
SMTPS - Encrypted communication with our Mail-servcer (postfix)
IMAPS - Encrypted communication with our Mail-storage-server (Dovect)

sect3.para: In principle we could use the same key-pair for all these channels but in our setup we will use one key-pair for the Web-server and one key-pair for both the SMTPS and the IMAPS channels. The motivation for this is that the Web-server is one standalone server which could be used for a multitude of applications and the SMTPS/IMAPS channels logically belong together as one application. The public HTTPS key should also be distributed to Web-clients wanting to connect to us without getting browser warnings.

In addition we will create our own CA (root) certificate that we will use to sign all these key-pairs (certificates). Our hierarchy of certificates is shown in . The public root certificate should also be distributed to all clients for them to verify the other certificates.
We should also make a note of the key length here. By default openssl uses key lengths of 1024 bits. To protect your ordinary mail from the occasional snooping this is probably good enough.

However, for corporate level protection a key length of at least 2048 bits are recommended and for those who are paranoid a key of 4096 bits can be used. The main drawback of longer key length is the increased processing power it requires for decryption/ encryption.

note.para: From 2011 Microsoft has removed all 1024 bit root certificate from the distribution of its browser.

sect3.para: A valid question now is who signs the CA (root) certificate?

The answer is no-one. These certificates (key-pairs) are trusted because we say so (they are truly self-signed). They don't need higher authority, technically they have a flag inside them saying that "this is a trusted root certificate that doesn't need anyone else to vouch for it", hence we should trust it. This also means that when we install these root certificates we have to make sure we are installing them from a secure source that we trust. It could potentially be devastating if we were to install bogus root certificates that were controlled by an "evil" entity since they could potentially fool us into believing that a signed program was produced by a trusted party when it in fact could be a spy program.

Browsers, for example, come with a large set of root certificates from trusted sources as do OpenSuSE Linux distribution. In the case of OpenSuSE all trusted root certificates can be found under the directory /etc/ssl/certs/

All key-pairs are created using the openssl package and more specifically the “openssl” command using various options. As mentioned before the steps to create these keys (certificates) and doing the signing are not really difficult taken step by step (and is shown in .) but there are a number of steps to be taken and since even professional system administrators do this fairly seldom there is no point in committing all the detailed steps by memory.

Exactly for this reason there are a number of shell scripts floating around that lines up the commands needed to create all these certificates so one does not have to memorize all the steps in using the openssl library. The library and tool isn't exactly a user friendly so even professionals that deals with this library on a regular basis create there own utility script to make life easier. Unfortunately there isn't a set of “commonly agreed” utility scripts.

X.509/SSL/TSL certificates introduces several terms that must be understood. The most important is the Distinguished Name or DN. This is a unique name used to identify a particular certificate (and key) among all other 1000s of certificates in the world. Hence this must be unique to each certificate.

note.para: Beware that many SSL/TLS scripts floating around on the net are “Chinese whispers”. While they do work they use long since obsolete options and ways to do things that are no longer recommended (at least since 2004!). The reason is most likely that getting into the details of openssl is not something many people want to do. So finding a small script on the net that seems to do the job is good enough for most people and so the scripts (unfortunately) gets handed down to the next unsuspecting generation.
Again, in we show the proper modern way of handling openssl.

sect3.para: The DN is in turn made up of several fields such as organization name, unit within the organization, town, state etc. One field in the DN with very special meaning is the Common Name (or CN) field. This is used to identify the domain name (e.g. www.example.com) that is used to access the server where the certificate is used. If the CN differs from the URL that is used to access (for example) a Web-server you will normally get a warning that the authenticity of the server cannot be guaranteed. The CN is normally the fully qualified domain name (FQD) of the server. This poses some problems if the server is multi-homed, i.e. it can be accessed using different URLs, for example if both http://www.example.com and http://example.com are valid aliases. For this reasons there are extensions (in the X.509 standard) that makes it possible to add a number of aliases that the certificate should still be valid under (all aliases must still resolve to the same IP address though). How this is done is further described in . This is also an example of quite important information that is not commonly found on all the sites that discuss certificate handling.

The final step after creating all these certificates is to install the public CA (the root certificate) in our browser and mail client(s) to avoid warnings about untrusted certificates. This is strictly speaking not necessary but will avoid annoying warnings whenever you try to connect to your server, for example via a Web-browser.

note.para: A X.509/SSL/TSL certificate is not exactly identical to the public key. A certificate acts as a container for the public key and adds additional information such as who has issued the certificate and who has guaranteed the authenticity of the certificate and various other information such as how long the certificate is valid for.
If you want more information about a certificate openssl can display a more detailed textual printout. The following examples shows how to printout information in various situations.
To view information on the public certificate use the command
To view the technical details about the private key use the command
$> openssl rsa –noout –text –in mykey.pemTo view the details about a certificate request use the command

sect3.para: In the following description of the setup of Apache and Dovecot/postfix we have made use of the utility scripts that are available with OpenSuSE since this is the easiest way to get up and running without having to learn too much details about openssl. However, after you have a working setup we strongly encourage you to read through . where a more satisfying and complete description and setup of SSL/TLS certificates can be found. Reading through this appendix will hopefully take away part of the “black-magic” surrounding this area.

sect1.title: Setting up Apache http-server
sect1.para: To setup Apache we will first create and enable SSL/TLS certificates to be able to connect over https:// protocol to the server. After this we will define a separate document root for the HTTPS traffic and finally enable PHP5 for the secured version of Apache.
To separate the normal document root (that is accessed through http://) and the secure root (accessed through https://) we will also create a new secure document root at “/srv/www/ssl-htdoc”.

In the following we will assume that you have installed Apache v2.x together with the Apache PHP5 module through SuSE package management. Please make sure that you can access some test page using normal HTTP traffic to your Web-server before continuing.

sect2.title: Creating self-signed SSL/TLS certificate for Apache
sect2.para: Creating SSL/TLS certificates for the https:// protocol is as mentioned above straightforward but a bit tedious. The good news here is that in OpenSuSE 11.4 there is a command script that does all the steps involved in creating certificates semi-automatically using openssl, “gensslcert”. The built-in help in this script will show all necessary options for the certificates. So running

will give you the list of all options. In the example command line below we will assume that the server resides in Sweden (country code SE) and accessed through the IP address 192.168.0.50 (in the address range reserved for a local net not directly connected to the internet). The IP address specified on the command line is rather important (it is the CN name) as described in the previous section on SSL/TLS. When your browser accesses the server it will check that the certificate it received from the server belongs to exactly the server accessed by this URL. If there is a mismatch you will get a warning that the site should not be trusted (since the certificate could have been made out to another server and then just copied). This might cause some irritation since a server could be multi-homed, i.e. accessed via different paths or URLs. You might for example have a dynamic DNS setup so you can access your home server from anywhere in the world with a domain name of your choice, say “http://myserver.dyndns.com” but you could also access the sever in your home local network, for example as http://192.168.0.50.

So there is a choice to be made here. The domain name which you most often use to connect to your server should be used in the certificate (as given in the Common Name field). This way you get the fewest warnings when connecting to your server.

tip.para: With a more advanced setup for the certificate handling, described in , it is possible to setup several “alias” addresses for the same server to avoid this kind of irritating warning messages.

sect2.para: in our case we will use the IP as the common name for the server certificate so we call the utility script as:

This will create both our own trusted root certificate as well as the certificate for the server itself and then sign the certificates with our own root certificate. Our self-signed certificate will be valid for 10 years (~3650 days) and valid for the server that is accessed by the IP address 192.168.0.50. Our CA (root) certificate will be valid for roughly 20 years (~7000 days). It is still possible to access the server through other URLSs for example by its name (if you have put it in your “/etc/hosts” file or even have a local DNS setup) but the browser will issue a warning in that case that it cannot validate the authenticity of the server. The exact wording of the warning (and appearance) is browser dependent.
After you have run this script the necessary certificate files will be stored under various subdirectories “/etc/apache2/ssl.*” as shown in .
After the certificates have been created we must now enable SSL and set the document root correctly in Apache for the virtual host which will handle the incoming HTTPS connections.

sect2.title: Enabling SSL in the OpenSuSE configuration
sect2.para: Many of the configurations in the apache configuration script templates available with OpenSuSE have conditional statements whether SSL/TSL is enabled or not. This is controlled by a single flag stored in the configuration file “/etc/sysconfig/apache2”. In this file a number of variables define the setup for Apache. Here there are two variables that must be correctly set.

First the string variable APACHE_MODULES has to have “ssl” defined in the list of modules to be loaded. This variable is automatically set by Yast when you install Apache. If this module is missing there is a risk that you have not properly installed Apache with the necessary mod_ssl module.
Secondly the SSL flag must be set as a Apache server flag as
This must be set in order to enable the conditional “<IfDefine SSL>” statements to be executed in various configuration files.

note.para: To avoid manually editing /etc/sysconfig/apache2 in oder to enable or disable Apache modules or flags there are two command line tools that can do this, "a2enflag" and "a2enmod". These two command are used to disable/enable flags and modules in syconfig file.
For example the following two commands would add both the SSL flag and the module mod_ssl to the configuration file
To list all the currently enabled modules use the following command (the modules listed below are just examples and does not necessary reflect what must be loaded.)

para.screen: $> a2enmod -l actions alias auth_basic authn_file authz_host authz_groupfile \ authz_default authz_user autoindex cgi dir env expires proxy \ proxy_http proxy_html include log_config mime negotiation \ setenvif ssl userdir rewrite php5 dav dav_svn

sect2.title: Setting up a virtual host for HTTPS
sect2.para: What we want to do now is to make use of the certificates we created and have Apache look in the alternative document root “/srv/www/ssl-htdocs” when the server receives a request over “https://”

note.para: Strictly speaking there is no need to have a separate document root for HTTPS. It is possible to use the same document root as for normal HTTP traffic. However, for security reasons it is better to put pages that should only be accessible through the HTTPS in a separate root to avoid the risk that they are accessed through the normal HTTP protocol by mistake.

sect2.para: We will be very short in the description here since configuring Apache is not necessarily very difficult but requires a lot of text to explain all the details. So in this context we will just show what is needed with a minimum of explanations (there are entire books written on Apache configurations to consult). In . there is a also a complete configuration file as an example.
To setup the new document root for the https:// connection start with the following four steps:

listitem.para: Switch to root user
Create the enw document root for HTTPS://
Change to directory /etc/apache2/vhosts.d
Copy the template config file for an SSL-enabled server as a starting point

sect2.para: We shall now edit the vhost-ssl.conf file so that Apache finds the certificates we want to use and the new document root we just created. Find the following variables in the configuration file we just copied (vhost-ssl.conf) and change them as shown below
sect2.programlisting:
# Setup document root and server name DocumentRoot “/srv/www/ssl-htdocs” ServerName 192.168.0.50:443
# Setup log files ErrorLog /var/log/apache2/ssl-error.log TransferLog /var/log/apache2/ssl-access.log
# Tell Apache where to find the certificate files SSLCertificateFile /etc/apache2/ssl.crt/192.168.0.50-server.crt SSLCertifictaeKeyFile /etc/apache2/ssl.key/192.168.0.50-server.key SSLCertifictaeChainFile /etc/apache2/ssl.crt/192.168.0.50-ca.crt
sect2.para: After you have changed this we need to tell Apache to accept the new document root. Add the following lines just after the TransferLog directive (as long as it appears within the “<VirtualHost _default_:443> … </VirtualHost>” it is really irrelevant where you put it)

para.programlisting: <Directory “/srv/www/ssl-htdocs”> Options None AllowOverride All Order allow,deny Allow from all </Directory>

Any additional configuration files added to your Apache setup (possible by Yast) will be read also for our encrypted setup in this way.

Please look at the (surprisingly readable) Apache documentation for a more detailed explanation of possible setups. It is also highly likely that in the end you may want to tailor the setup according to your own needs (most likely you want to change the “Options” parameter for the document root directory, for example to allow symbolic links to be followed).

sect1.title: Setting up Dovecot
sect1.para: The reason to start with Dovecot rather than postfix is twofold. One is that postfix will make use of the Dovecot SSL/TLS certificates (as shown in ) and the second is that postfix will use Dovecot SASL service to authenticate incoming SMTP requests. SASL stands for Simple Authentication and Security Layer and is a standardized protocol to handle for example logins. The reason for this is that we want incoming SMTP traffic to be authenticated forcing users to log in before being able to send mails through our SMTP(s) server. Since postfix does not provide any authentication service by itself it must make use of some service provided by another component, Dovecot in this case.
The reason for re-using the SSL/TLS certificates from Dovecot in postfix is partly laziness; Dovecot comes with a small script that makes the creation of certificates very easy.

tip.para: We also remind you of the more complete description on how to use openssl directly in Appendix E. to create a certificate hierarchy with a bit more control that comes from better understanding. But for now we make use of the utility script that comes with Doevcot2 since it is the easier way for a newcomer to do what needs to be done.

sect1.para: In the following we assume that you have installed Dovecot2 through Yast. Before continue please make sure that you install dovecot 2.0.x and not 1.x. For some bizarre reason SuSE still uses 1.x as the default version of Dovecot (instead of Dovecot2).

note.para: The script that comes with Dovecot does roughly the same step as the previously used gensslcert but stores the resulting certificate files in a different directory and also uses the *.pem endings instead of *crt/*key (see the section on SSL/TLS certificates for an explanation of *pem vs. *crt/*.key suffixes)

sect2.title: Creating dovecot SSL/TLS certificates
sect2.para: In order to use IMAPS we must first create SSL certificates and keys in much the same way as we did for the Apache. In fact, it would be perfectly possible to reuse the exact same keys and certificates that we created for the web-server. Just watch out for the names of the certificate files.

However as we discussed previously we will use a separate set of certificates for Dovecot and postfix. For this purpose Dovecot includes a small shell script that will call all the necessary openssl commands in much the same way as gensslcert did for the web-server. This utility script is called mkcert.sh and is found in the directory /usr/share/doc/packages/dovecot. To put correct default values in the certificate first open and edit the file dovecot-openssl.cnf (that is in the same directory). This configuration file contains the values used for names and organization in the certificate. Open the file in an editor and change the setting to match your setup.

Before you run mkcert.sh you probably also want to edit the end of the file so that the generated certificate is valid for longer than a year which (unfortunately) is hard code in the end of the script. Change the argument “–days 365” in the script to something a bit longer, for example 3650 days ≈ 10 years.

sect2.title: Testing the dovecot configuration
sect2.para: To verify that the basics of our IMAP server works we can try to manually connect on port 993, however since that requires a setup of an SSL encrypted connection we cannot directly connect to the port (we need to use openssl s_client). So as an alternative we can (as a test) enable normal IMAP in 10-master.conf. Do this by un-commenting the line #port = 143 in the IMAP section at the top of the file. Now restart Dovecot in the same way as before.
We can then login to dovecot using a basic telnet connection
sect2.screen: $> telnet localhost 143 Trying ::1… Connected to localhost.Escape character is ‘^]’.* * OK [CAPABILITY MIAP4rev1 LITERAL+ SASL-IR LOGIN-REFERRALS \ ID ENABLE IDLE STARTTLS AUTH=PLAIN] Dovecot ready.
sect2.para: The last line indicates that Dovecot is running and has accepted our connection. In order to do anything else we must login using a user in the system.

The IMAP login command is login <user> <password> So if you continue the previous telnet session by logging in using a known user and password (this user must exist in your system and should have a proper mailbox under /srv/mail/) you should now get a reply resembling
sect2.screen: 10 login tstuser tstpassword 10 OK [CAPABILITY ….] Logged in
sect2.para: If you wonder about the "10" in the beginning of the command this is just an arbitrary tag for the command. All IMAP commands has to be preceded by a user defined tag. When the IMAP server gives back a reply it will always use the tag for the command that caused this output. Tags allows us to know from which command an output comes from. It is possible to give several commands in a row and some might take long time so there is no guarantee that the servers reply will be in the same order as the given commands. Dovecot ignores the actual characters in the tag so it can be completely arbitrary.
The next step is to list available folders for this user
sect2.screen: 10 list “” * * LIST (\HasNoChildren) “.” INBOX” 10 OK List completed.
sect2.para: The above command also makes sure that dovecot can access the folder (in our case /srv/mail/tstuser)
If you get this far chances are high that dovecot setup is correct. After we have configured postfix and we actually have some mails in our inbox we will manually retrieve them as well.
Finally disconnect from dovecot by logging out
sect2.screen: 10 logout BYE Logging out. 10 OK Logout completed.

sect2.para: In order to drastically (~x1000) speed up full text searches (fts) of mailboxes it is possible to have Dovecot maintain a full text index for each mail folder. The easiest way to do this is to use Dovecots own full text search engine “Squat” (“Search Query Answer Tool”).

The index is initially created the very first time a search is performed on a directory so this first time will take extra time and memory depending on the number of mails in the directory. Thereafter Dovecot will update the index incrementally as changes are made to the mail directories.

sect1.title: Setting up postfix
sect1.para: To remind our self where we are in the process we clarify that after setting up postfix we will be able to send mails from our own machine by connecting to a running postfix daemon via the SMTP(S) protocol.

All relevant postfix configuration files can be found in the /etc/postfix/ directory. In the first instance we will setup postfix using a regular SMTP connection without the added complexity of a SSL/TLS certificate. Once we get this working we will modify the configuration to use the same key and certificate we created for Dovecot. This will work just fine as long as Dovecot and the SMTP server are running on the same host. If they are running on separate hosts you will need to create a unique certificate for postfix.
In postfix there are two files in the /etc/postfix directory. we need to update:

listitem.para: main.cf - This is where all settings are stored, one huge parameter file
master.cf - This file controls what helper processes are started and on what ports they are listening.

caution.para: The changes you make manually in the postfix configuration might come into conflict if you later on decide to use YAST setup for the mail server. So don’t use the YAST setup once you have manually configured postfix (into perfection!). Actually we would recommend against using YAST mail server setup for any serious mail server since the tuning possibilities are near to zero.

Also, please be careful when editing the configuration file and watch out for setting the correct server variable. Sender or receiver, i.e. with prefix smtp_<variable> or smtpd_<variable> this is a common source of errors that can be surprisingly time consuming to find.

sect2.title: User authentication in postfix
sect2.para: Before we continue we need to touch upon how postfix handles user authentication. When do we need that? By default postfix restricts who can use our server to send mail based on IP address. It will allow clients on the same sub-network as the server. However, with mobile usage we will most likely connect to our postfix server through our gateway and then the gateway will forward our request to the server. Hence the request looks like it is coming from our sub-network (our gateway) and will be allowed. This would then allow anyone that knows our official IP address to the gateway (and the port to use) to use our SMTP server to send mail that looks like it is coming from us! This is what is known as an open relay and is something really bad.

So, we need a way to authenticate users before they are allowed to send mail via our SMTP server. By itself postfix has no built-in method for this. Instead it is constructed to use an external library which implements an API known as SASL (Simple Authentications and Security Layer). The SASL library is a completely independent of postfix. There are several available providers of a compliant SASL library (for example the SASL authentication daemon saslauthd). The good news here is that Dovecot provides one possible implementation of it. Since we already have Dovecot installed it seems a good idea to use it. As you recall we made some provisions for this when we configured Dovecot (even though we didn't explain the details at the time).
So after we have configured postfix to use the Dovecot SASL the following happens when a user connects.

listitem.para: Postfix send the authentication details through the SASL API to Dovecot

Dovecot receives the authentication details and uses the configured way to lookup the user details. By default dovecot uses the Linux PAM framework which normally is configured to check the user and password from the shadow password file. This requires all mail users to also have an account on the server. Dovecot can also use other methods such as an LDAP server or even a database with all the user credentials stored. The main advantage with storing users in a DB is that they do not need to have user accounts on the server.
Dovecot returns fail or succeed to postfix which based on this knows whether to accept or reject the incoming call.

sect2.para: In this way SASL is able to authenticate remote users that want to send mail through our SMTP server.

There is still one problem with our authentication setup in that the user and passwords are sent in plain text over the network. For automatic network sniffers this is a gold mine since the harvesting of valid user/passwords combos is what spammers are after. The way to protect our conversation is to use SSL/TLS encryption of the communication between the client and our server in the same way we protect our IMAP and https:// traffic.

note.para: SSL (Secure Socket Layer) was renamed TLS (Transport Layer Security) by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) as of version 3.1 There are technically some differences between SSL and TLS but for all practical reasons they are the same.

sect3.title: Rewriting sender addresses
sect3.para: If a mail is sent from the local user on a server that is not directly connected to the internet it will have a domain name that in most cases are “fake”, for example joe@localhost.nil (this will of course depend on what name you have given the server). The problem with this is twofold. First the recipient cannot answer to this address and secondly most mail servers requires that the from-address is a valid (can be looked up in DNS) to forward the mail at all.

To correct this situation postfix has the ability to rewrite your “bad” addresses to something the recipient can actually answer to. In fact, a lot of the complexity in postfix comes from the various ways of rewriting addresses. Here we will just use the most basic rewrite functionality. For a fuller (and very readable) discussion on the rewrite options in postfix consult the postfix HowTo “Postfix Address Rewriting” available on the postfix website.
This type of address rewriting is also known as address “masquerading” (for obvious reasons).

In order to have postfix translate the “bad” mail address to a “good” address a file with mappings between “bad” and “good” must be created. sect3.title: Accessing an encrypted server
sect3.para: Historically a separate port has been used for the encrypted version of the SMTP protocol when SSL was used. With SSL (and not TLS!) this is needed since the entire conversation is encrypted so the server listening on the port has to use encryption from the start. The only real user noticeable difference between SSL and TLS is that with the modern TLS it is possible to start the conversation non-encrypted and as soon as both client and server has agreed to use encryption the rest of the conversation is encrypted. One of the big advantages with TLS is therefore that it is possible to use the same port for both encrypted and non-encrypted traffic (as defined by RFC 3207) .
This means that we now have a choice on how we setup the actual access to the server over the encrypted connections.

listitem.para: Use a dedicated port (old way) with SSL or
Use the same port with TLS

sect3.para: For all modern installation it is strongly recommended to use the modern way with the same port using TLS.

sect3.title: Using a dedicated port for encrypted traffic
sect3.para: Again, this is NOT the recommended way but is included for completion. Unless you know that some clients only support this way you should not implement this.

Originally port 465 was used as the separate SSL port for encrypted SMTP or SMTPS (sometimes also referred to as SSMTP). Unfortunately this port assignment was never made official as far as IANA recognized port numbers are. Instead it is registered for URD – “URL Rendesvous Directory for SSM” by Cisco.

In addition the original intention of port 465 was to let SMTP servers forward mail between each other over an encrypted channel. It was never intended to be used by mail clients to talk to the server directly. For this purpose another port was to be used, port 587 “Message submission” (see RFC 2476).

So using this older setup an SMTP server was really supposed to be listening on three ports. Port 25 for normal unencrypted traffic both from other servers and from clients, port 465 to allow other servers to communicate and finally port 587 to allow mail clients to submit new mails.

In reality most servers only use two port, one for unencrypted and one for encrypted traffic. Even though technically incorrect most servers use port 465 for use with SMTPS (both from clients and other severs).

For a small home based server (which is not a real MX server connected directly to the internet as a official mail server) it doesn't really matter if you choose the common (but incorrect) port 465 or port 587 as long as you configure your clients correctly on which port they should use to send mails. The only thing you need to watch out for when using port 465 is that since this is not an officially assigned port for SMTPS which means some extra steps as described below.

sect3.para: Since port 465 is not an officially recognized port for SMTPS we must either update /etc/services to be able to use the symbolic name “smtps” for the port in our master.cnf postfix or use the port number directly.

So the next step is to tell postfix to listen on this port and enable the manger process that handles the TLS connection for postfix. This is done by editing master.cf and first removing the comment for the line:

para.programlisting: smtps inet n - n - - SMTPD –o smtpd_tls_wrappermode=yes

para.emphasis: Using port 587 for encrypted SMTP traffic

sect3.para: Since port 587 is an officially recognized port there is no need to update /etc/services . The only update needed is to remove the comments in master.cnf for the two lines

If you look in the master.cnf file you will also see that by default some optional parameters are give directly on the command line. The parameters are mirrors of the ones given in the main.cnf but will take precedence. The command line parameters are useful when you need different set of parameters for different ports.

Actually port 587 should really be used for submitting emails even if no encryption is used. Unfortunately many commercial providers do not follow this recognized standard and just assumes that both clients and other servers would contact them on port 25.
If you want to use port 587 for submission with only optional encryption for those client requesting this just remove the “smtpd_tls_auth_only = yes” option and SSL/TLS encryption will be optional.

sect3.title: Using the same port for both encrypted and non-encrypted traffic
sect3.para: This is the recommended way for a modern secure SMTP server setup.

With this method no extra ports are needed. Instead the normal port 25 is used for both encrypted and non encrypted traffic. When a client first connects to the server it will notice the by the servers response that TLS is supported (by the STARTTLS response code) and if the client is also capable of TLS encryption it might then ask the server to continue the rest of the conversation using SSL/TLS encryption.
To enable this method it suffices to enable the tlsmgr by uncommenting the line
in master.cnf

This might seem contradictory to what we recommended in the previous paragraph regarding the use of port 587. Technically you would be correct. The advantage is that some poorly written clients will only support port 25. In addition keeping as few ports open as possible is a good thing from a security point.

This is simply case where there simply is no single one correct answer. The official standard stipulates one thing but years of de-facto standard shows something else. Most (all?) ISP do not even allow incoming traffic on port 587 (which they really should!) and many clients only support port 25 for unencrypted submission and port 465 for encrypted submission (which technically is the wrong way of doing it).

sect1.title: Setting up fetchmail
sect1.para: Fetchmail:s role is to fetch mail from remote hosts to our server and deliver the fetched mail locally. In order to fetch mail we must first setup a configuration file for fetchmail with the remote servers and there credentials where we want to fetch mail, this configuration file is /etc/fetchmailrc.
After fetchmail has logged in it will deliver the mails locally to our SMTP server just as if the mail had come from some remote SMTP server connecting to us.

There is one thing to keep in mind here though and that is that fetchmail only handles password when fetching mail. It cannot handle passwords in the local delivery. This means that our postfix setup must accept incoming mails that should be delivered locally without password (which is the normal). Since we have specified smtpd_recipient_restrictions with the option permit_mynetworks This will allow fetchmail to store mail locally without providing a password.

To be really secure we should restrict this further by only allowing access from within the server itself. This can be done by making sure that mynetworks_style=host is set and make sure that mynetworks is empty since that configuration variable has precedence (if that is set the mynetworks_style will be ignored).

sect2.title: Configuring fetchmail
sect2.para: In the documentation for fetchmail there are several examples on how to setup a basic configuration. So in this section we will show some examples of more complex setup which isn't available in the fetchmail documentation.
The advantage (if any) with fetchmail configuration syntax is that it is quite "chatty" and can be read almost as an English sentence.

Let's start with a very basic example. Assuming that the remote server is called “remotemail.com” and the server uses POP3 (not IMAP). Furthermore we assume the username is “joe” (both remote and local) and the password is “secret.
The following configuration line will handle this case:

para.programlisting: poll remotemail.com proto pop3 user "joe" there \ with password "secret" is "joe" here;

sect2.para: Let's now do a slightly more complex setup. In this setup we are connecting to an IMAP server over SSL/TSL (meaning that we need to connect on port 993) and we want to collect mail from both the “Inbox” folder as well as the “Junk” mail folder back to our server.
Furthermore we want to permanently delete mails that are rejected as spams by our own postfix server when fetchmail tries to deliver it.

para.programlisting:
defaults user "joe@remotemail.com" is "joe" set no softbounce antispam 501 bad-header accept
poll imap.remotemail.com with proto IMAP port 993: SSL folder 'inbox','Junk' password "secret";

sect2.para: There are a couple of unusual thing in this setup.

listitem.para: To make it more readable we first set up some default values that apply to all defined servers. We use this to first set the user we are collecting mail from. The second option requires some more explanations. If we fetch a mail from the remote server and when we try to deliver it to our own postfix server it is refused since it is considered a wrongly formatted mail. In this case fetchmail will normally leave the mail on the remote server. With this option set fetchmail will remove the mail from the remote server even when it was rejected by our own server, effectively deleting the mail without anyone ever receiving it.
This might sound like a bad thing to do. However mail that are so wrongly formatted that postfix refuses to accept it as a proper mail are to 99.999% spams.

The antispam 501 line tells fetchmail to interpret an 501 error (Bad address syntax) from the local postfix server not as an error but as a signal that the delivered mail is interpreted as a spam by postfix. It will then discard the message and since “set no softbounce” is in effect. The mail will then also be deleted from the remote server.

A common cause of this is that postfix with default settings refuses addresses which begin by an “-“ (hyphen). This might be unusual but it is actually allowed (see RFC 5321, RFC 5322) so in this case postfix is a bit picky.
The “bad-header accept” command allows fetchmail to collect mail even if some of the headers are incorrect.
We then specify that we connect to the IMAP server on port 993 and enable SSL.
To get mail from several folders we use the “folder” command and then just list the folders we want to collect the mail from

sect2.para: Before starting fetchmail check that you are happy with the default configuration in /etc/sysconfig/fetchmail such as poll interval. (Just keep in mind that some ISP gets a bit unhappy if you try to poll there server every minute or so.)
