sect1.title: Setting up spamassassin
sect1.para: Spamassassin is a Perl based program/script that uses statistical analysis of text to determine the likelihood that a certain mail is a spam or legitimate mail. Spamassassin is one of the oldest spam filter but has been regularly updated and is good enough for small scale home based server. The main complaints for a large scale setup of is not the quality of the analysis but rather that it requires quite a lot of computing power and can take several ms to scan each mail. In a large (several thousand mails an hour) setup this can become a bottleneck and a separate server might nede to be deployd for this prpose..

However there is one way to speed things up and reduce the system load and that is the spamd/spamc daemon/client setup. This allows spamassassin to remain running in the memory and avoids starting up a Perl process and shut it down for each mail to be scanned. This is also installed by default (but not enabled). To call the resident daemon the client spamc is used. This is also the client program we call from within our procmail script to run the mails through the spam filter.
To enable the spamd daemon either enabled it via Yast System Services (runlevel) editor or via the command line
After installing spamassassin via Yast there are several places where the configuration files reside.

listitem.para: /usr/share/spamassassin - This is where all the static rules are stored that gets installed with spamassassin. In here is also the file local.cf which is the only file that should be modified for local preferences since all other files will be overwritten in case of an upgrade. However it is recommended tht you do not make any modifications here. Instead use the config file under /etc (see next bullet)
/etc/mail/spamassassin/local.conf - This is only the proper place to do local modifications for server wide adjustments
<user home>/.spamassassin/user_prefs - This is the proper file to set user specific modifications

sect1.para: When spamassassin reads the configuration files it first reads the files under /usr then the files under /etc and finnaly the users home directory. If any file has the same name the later version will be added to the previous version so any changes in a later file will override previous changes.

The default settings are usually good enough for the majority of users but you may want to lower the default spam threshold of a score of 5.0 to something a bit lower, say 4. This change could be made in /etc/mail/spamassassin/local.conf to affect all users on the server.

It is important to understand that spamassassin by itself does not sort mails in any way. It simply adds a few headers in the mail indicating how likely the mail is to be a spam. It is then up to the rules in the procmail script to interpret these headers to determine if the mail should be put in the spamfolder or be received as a regular mail. The specific headers added by spamassassin are shown in table .

Spamassassin is in our setup run by procmail as an external program and run as the user who is receiving the mail. Procmail puts each mail who's size is less than a predetermined size through spamassassin and then looks in the headers to determine if the mail should be put in the spam folder, possible deleted forever or just forwarded to the normal inbox or perhaps some other mail folder. Review the procmail configuration in the next section for how this is done.

The reason to limit the size of mail we put through spamassassin to avoid having (for example) large mails with multimedia content to be run through spamassassin since that would consume a lot of time and spam mails are never (well almost) that large so that would just be a waste of server time.

sect2.title: Configuring spamassassin Bayes auto learning
sect2.para: Apart from the static analysis on headers and content of the mail spamassassin also has the ability to learn the particular words in typical spams. This later on helps spamassassin identify spams.
Bayes auto learning is enabled by default but you should also check that it is by checking that bayes_auto_learn 1

By default spamassassin learns word from mails and learns them as either spam or non-spam ("ham") depending on thresholds defined in the configuration file. By default these thresholds are rather high to avoid learning from false positive. You can be more aggressive here and for example use the following lower thresholds values.
sect2.programlisting:
# Use Bayesian classifier (default: 1) # # use_bayes 1
# Bayesian classifier auto-learning (default: 1) # # bayes_auto_learn 1
# Mail which scores outside this range will be fed back into SpamAssassin's # learning system automatically, to train the Bayesian scanner. ifplugin Mail::SpamAssassin::Plugin::AutoLearnThreshold bayes_auto_learn_threshold_nonspam 0.01 bayes_auto_learn_threshold_spam 6.0 endif # Mail::SpamAssassin::Plugin::AutoLearnThreshold
sect2.para: The above changes can be made either in /etc/mail/spamassassin/local.conf to take affect side wide or in the ~/.spamassassin/user_prefs file to affect only a specific user.
If you have a folder with eihter spam or ham you can also instruct spamassassin to learn from that collection with the use of the "sa-learn" command. For example as

sect2.para: To verify that the spamassassin daemon is running we can do a simple manual test by running some nonsense text through the spamassassin client spamc which in turns calls on spamd.
You should now get a fairly long reply with the headers in table clearly visible in a format that (almost) looks like the raw format of a mail.

A graphical indication with ‘*’ to indicate the computed spam score. Each ‘*’ represents one integer score.
A detailed list with the numerical score, required score and list of tests that indicates that this might be a spam.

sect1.title: Setting up procmail
sect1.para: When postfix receives a mail it will by default store the mail in the mail spool directory (either “/var/spool/mail/user” or “/var/mail/user”).

Postfix offers no possibility of post-processing of the received mails. For example to run the received mails through a spamfilter (like spamassassin) and put all identified spams in a separate mail folder.

To solve this we tell postfix to send all the received mails that should be locally delivered through another program, in our case procmail. It is this program that will act as a Local Delivery Agent, LDA, and perform the last stage when incoming mails are store on disk.

sect2.title: Configuration file
sect2.para: Procmail is controlled with (yet another) configuration file which by default is in the home directory of the user receiving the mail .procmailrc) . The configuration file will contain rules on how to process the incoming mails, such as storing mails based on different criteria in different folders. It is even possible to have certain mails automatically trigger other external programs. A typical use of this would be a server where users can send a one line mail to have some useful information automatically sent back.
In order to tell postfix to send incoming mails to procmail we must add the following line in the postfix config file (/etc/postfix/main.cf)

The next step is to setup the configuration file for procmail. Since it is possible to write an entire book on how to write procmail filtering rule we will keep this example simple. The example rule file below will do the following:

listitem.para: we will enable logging in a separate log file for each user under the /tmp directory
if the mail is judged to be “normal” spam we store it in the folder “Junk”
if the mail have a very high spam score we just discard them by deleting them forever
if the mail has the word “Newsletter” in the subject or comes from a sender “*.news.com” we put it in a separate mail folder “Newsletters”
otherwise we store it in the default inbox

sect2.para: The home page for procmail has many more receipts that you can take directly. For example “Out of office” style of automatic replies.

Unfortunately the syntax for procmail configuration is not exactly intuitive (anyone who think that has spent too much time with mail servers) but the basic structure in this example file will get you a good start and will serve a good start for your own experiments. It would bring this tutorial too far off track to become a “How To Write procmail Filter rules” as well. Refer to the procmail documentation for details.
In we also show some more example of procmail configuration recipes.

example.title: Template for a procmail configuration file
example.programlisting:
#--------------------------------------------- # Standard setup for extra logging #--------------------------------------------- VERBOSE=on LOGABSTRACT=all LOGFILE=/tmp/procmail-${LOGNAME}-`date +%Y%m`.log MAILDIR=/srv/mail/${LOGNAME} DEFAULT=${MAILDIR}/ INBOX=${MAILDIR}/
#--------------------------------------------- # Subfolders to filter mails in. # REMEMBER TO PUT TRAILING '/' AT # THE END # to mark the folders as being in maildir format #--------------------------------------------- SPAM=${MAILDIR}/.Junk/ NEWSLETTERS=${MAILDIR}/.newsletters/
##-------------------------------------------- ## End of setup. Now comes all the filer ## rules. ##--------------------------------------------
#--------------------------------------------- # FILTER for Newsletters. #--------------------------------------------- :0 ^Subject:.*Newsletter ^From:.*news.com { } :0 E $NEWSLETTERS
#--------------------------------------------- # FILTER for spamassassin #--------------------------------------------- :0 * < 512000 | /usr/bin/spamc #--------------------------------------------- # Discard all spams with score >= 15 #--------------------------------------------- :0 * !^X-Spam-Level: \*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*\*.* * !^X-Spam-Status: Yes, score=1[5-9]\.[0-9] * !^X-Spam-Status: Yes, score=[2-9][0-9]\.[0-9] { } :0 E /dev/null
#--------------------------------------------- # Put all remaining spams in Junk folder. # NOTE: This assumes spamassassin is configured # to set the X-Spam-Flag: YES for identified # spams. #--------------------------------------------- :0 * ^X-Spam-Flag: YES $SPAM
#--------------------------------------------- # Send the remaing mails to the inbox #--------------------------------------------- :0 $DEFAULT

note.para: By default procmail only supports “AND” rules, i.e. if you add a number of conditions before an action all of them has to be fulfilled for the action to be performed.
One of the most frequent questions newcomers to procmail have is therefore how to write “OR” rules, i.e. a rule that states that

para.code: if condition1 or condition2 is true then do action

note.para: The way around this is to realize that

para.code: “if A or B then do C”

note.para: is equivalent to

para.code: “if (not A) and (not B) then do nothing else do C”.

note.para: Any book on Boolean logic will give more details on this subject.

appendix.title: Postfix configuration examples
appendix.para: One key to configure postfix SMTPD access is to understand the configurations directive smtpd_recipient_restrictions. Below are two examples on how this can be used. Remember that the order of the settings in this configuration is important. Postfix will execute them sequentially

sect1.title: Example 1
sect1.para: The default settings will only allow anyone on the same subnetwork as the server to send relay mail through
sect1.programlisting:
mynetworks_style = subnet # only allow clients on the same subnet to connect
smtpd_recipient_restrictions = permit_mynetworks reject_unauth_destination

sect1.title: Example 2
sect1.para: Changing the mynetwork_style to only allow password less logins originating from the same server and require (SASL) password from all other logins are safer and can be done by this
sect1.programlisting:
mynetworks_style = host
smtpd_recipient_restrictions = permit_mynetworks permit_sasl_authenticated reject_unauth_destination

sect1.title: Example 3
sect1.para: Allow clients on the local machine (host) to connect and send relay mails without logging in. Force external clients to use SSL/TLS before allowing them to login.

mynetworks_style = host
# sasl smtpd_sasl_auth_enable = yes
# tls # smtpd_tls_security_level = may smtpd_tls_loglevel = 1 smtpd_tls_cert_file = </path/to/crt.crt> smtpd_tls_key_file = </path/to/key.key>

smtpd_recipient_restrictions = permit_mynetworks permit_sasl_authenticated reject_unauth_destination

sect1.para: This setup requires password authentication from both local and remote users but only require SSL/TLS from remote users

smtpd_recipient_restrictions = #allow anyone delivering mail to this host: permit_auth_destination #otherwise, allow authenticated connections from localhost check_client_access hash:/usr/local/etc/postfix/access_client #otherwise, demand both authentication and encryption: reject_plaintext_session permit_sasl_authenticated reject

appendix.title: Procmail recipes
appendix.para: The first line of a procmail filter always starts with “:0” and the remaining letters controls the filtering process.

For example “h” will only filter on the mail headers, “c” will make a copy of the mail so that it is available to filters after the current filter. If there is no “c” then the filter will consume the mail and processing stops here and no more filters will be applied to the mail.
Five good sites to find out more about how to write procmail recipes are:

listitem.para: http://pm-doc.sourceforge.net/doc/ (The official procmail documentation)
http://partmaps.org/era/procmail/mini-faq.html (Procmail FAQ)

sect1.title: The problem of filtering on the “Subject:” field
sect1.para: While at first it might seem simple enough to filter out certain mails with a specific subject either as spam or some other reason it is in practice a lot more complicated. The problem is that the subject does not always have to be in plain text. Instead it is very common to have the subject in either quoted printable or in base64. Such an encoded string looks like =?charset?format?encoded text?= (this format is more specifically described in RFC1522) and it can also be followed by some text in plain format and then again by some encoded text. For obvious reason a lot of spam uses this format to make it much more difficult to do simple text matching.
Unfortunately there is no easy way around this and procmail does not have any built in “decoding” functionality so this has to be done manually.

To help with this the following small perl script can be used as a helper script. This script has been floated on the net and the author is unfortunately unknown to me (if you know please let me now and the proper credit will be given)

Store this script a file and make the file executable (in the example below we will assume it is stored in /usr/bin/decode_subjheader ) In procmail we can then use formmail to first extract the subject header and then run that header through this perl script to get the decoded subject
For example the helper script can be used as:
sect1.programlisting: SUBJECT = `formail -xSubject: | /usr/bin/decode_subjheader` :0 * SUBJECT ?? (Newsletter.*) $NEWSLETTER
sect1.para: The recipe above will first extract the subject header from the mail and run it through our decoder perl script and then store the decoded header in the variable SUBJECT.
The details of the filtering rules are explained in Table

entry.para: If the filter matches then store it in the folder pointed to by the content of the variable

sect1.title: How to create filter that matches on any of several rules (creating an “OR” rule)
sect1.para: By default all matching rules in a filter need to apply before the action is taken. To create a rule which simulates an “OR” condition for the matching expression one has to make use of the “else” rule. This is done by executing an empty action “{ }” when all the conditions do NOT match and our “real” actions if this condition is not true. (This uses the fact that NOT( (NOT A) AND (NOT B)) = A OR B )
sect1.programlisting:
:0 hb * !<expression 1> * !<expression 2> { }
:0 E <action to be taken>

para.emphasis: Please note that there should be one space in the “{ }” empty statement!

sect1.para: So for example to store mail that comes from either ´"joe.r@gmail.com" or “helen.q@gmail.com” in a folder called “Friends” the following recipe could be used
sect1.programlisting:
0: hb * !^From:.*joe.r@gmail.com * !^From:.*Helen.q@gmail.com { }
:0 e $FRIENDS

sect1.title: Automatic expunging of old mails
sect1.para: Subscribing to non-personal mail like newsletters and mail lists tends to grow the mailbox quit a lot with information that usually is valid only for a short time. So having this kind of mail automatically deleted after a certain time period, say 2 weeks, is usually a good thing.

Dovecot provides a utility program called doveadm that can do exactly this. Among other things doveadm have a command "expunge" to delete all mails that matches a certain search criteria in a specified mailbox.

An example will clarify how this work. Assume we want to delete all mails older than two weeks in our "dovecot" mail folder. To do this we search and delete all mails that were stored in that mail folder more than fourteen days ago with the command:
sect1.programlisting: /usr/bin/doveadm expunge mailbox dev.dovecot savedbefore 14d
sect1.para: All messages older than 14 days in the mail folder “dev/dovecot” have now been deleted.
In Linux we can then setup a cron job that calls a script with these expunge command at regular intervals, say once a week or even once a day.

The search commands for doveadm are quite flexible so please look at the man page for other search options. The above line will cause all mails (both read and unread) to be deleted. One common modification is to have non read messages kept longer.
If we store the above line in a script as
sect1.programlisting: #!/bin/sh /usr/bin/doveadm expunge mailbox dev.dovecot savedbefore 14d
sect1.para: and store the script as, say, /usr/local/bin/user-expungemail we can then uses a cronjob to call this script a regular intervals. Having the jobs called every Wednesday and Sunday at 3 a´clock in the morning would for example require us to write
sect1.programlisting: 0 3 * * 3,7 /usr/local/bin/user-expungemail
sect1.para: If the server have multiple accounts each will need its own expunge cron job script run as the user that owns the account.

appendix.title: Create SSL/TLS keys and certificates with openssl
appendix.para: In the following we will create our own CA (Certification agency) that will sign all our public keys. This means that to avoid the warnings in browsers about untrusted certificate the CA certificate (our root certificate) should be imported into the browsers. As an example we will show how this is done for the Chrome browser at the end of this appendix.

The main purpose of this section is to show how the bare bones “openssl” command can be used to create certificates rather than relying on the simple but somewhat magical utility scripts we used in the main discussion. We recommend that one you have gotten over the initial chock of dealing with certificates this is actually a simpler method.

As convention we will use the extension *.pem for all keys (since this is the format they keys are in). To distinguish between the public (the certificate) and private key we will add “_public” and “_private” to the main name of the key-pair.

Some documentation uses the suffix “*.crt” and “*.key” for the public and private key in PEM format. However, our opinion is that the suffix should reflect the format of the file (in this case the PEM) format and the use of crt and key as suffixes make things unnecessary complicated. Especially since one might believe that “*.crt” and “*.key” are in themselves are new formats.
At the end of this walk-though we will have to generate the following key-pairs to use in our setup

listitem.para: This is our own “Root” certificate. This public key is implicitly trusted, i.e. it is trusted because we say so. No higher authority (but us) has sanctioned this key pair.
This is the keypair we will use with Apache when https connections are made
This is the keypair that will be used for both Dovecot2 as well as postfix to encrypt both IMAP and SMTP protocols into IMAPS and SMTPS
This is a keypair which makes it possible to access the server under several aliases. This if further described in section E.5

appendix.para: In the process of generating these targets there will also be some intermediate files that strictly speaking is not necessary to keep (but might come in handy later on as we shall see).
The process is now as follows

listitem.para: Create the CA key-pair as a root certificate, i.e. it will be “signed” by itself. It is trusted because we say so!
Handle the key-pair for https
Create the key-pair, private and public key
Prepare the public key to be signed by creating the “Certificate signing request” (CSR) based on the public key
Sign the public key with our CA private key
Handle the key-pair for dovecot and postfix
Create the key-pair, private and public key
Prepare the public key to be signed by creating the “Certificate signing request” (CSR) based on the public key
c. Sign the public key with our CA private key

appendix.para: Please read through the above steps again and make sure you understand the principle. (In practice the creation of the key-pair and the signing request is done in one step – but logically they are separate.)

caution.para: There is no shortage of description on the net on how to create so called self-signed certificates. However many of them are dated and based on very old ways of doing things which have just been inherited out of laziness and without propre understanding of the tools involved.

For example, many descriptions do not add the “-nodes” flag as we do in these examples. This will force a password to be created for the private key in certificates and since this is usually not wanted (as described below) one extra step is then required to remove the password. Hence making the description unnecessarily complicated. Another example of obsoleted usage is the option “nsCertType = server” in config files. This option is since long superseded and is not even necessary in our context. Again, adding complexity where none is needed. Another (very popular) complexity adder is to create the private key separately from the certificate request with another obsoleted command; “openssl genrsa”.

Yet another plain wrong way that many HowTo:s show is to create the initial serial number for the certificates in the database (that “openssl ca” keeps of all signed certificates ) by simply storing a number one in a file (usually by “echo 01 > serial”). Instead the option “-create_serial” should be given to let openssl initialize a random 128 bit serial number.

Dealing with SSL/TLS certificate introduces many new terms and takes a while getting used to especially since “openssl” is not exactly easy to use. It has evolved (together with the standards) for a long time and old options that are since long superseded remains. However, there is no need to make things more black magic than necessary and the way we show below is what we believe the absolute easiest way to accomplish what we need in the minimum number of steps.

sect1.title: The use of the term “self-signed certificates”
sect1.para: The term self-signed certificate has two distinct meanings. It could mean that we sign a certificate that we have generated our self with our own CA (root) certificate that we have either created (most likely) or bought (highly unlikely). This is the way we use the term self-signed certificate in this appendix.

It could also mean that we create a CA-type certificate which is (almost) a regular certificate that it not signed by anyone but have a flag inside it that says “trust me, because I say so – I’m a root certificate”. This is really what openssl means by self-signing, the certificate is signed by itself.
Many of the tools out there create this latter type of certificate to avoid having to create a separate CA (root certificate)

sect1.title: Preparations
sect1.para: When reading the description below you need to watch out for the order of the argument to openssl. Sometimes it doesn’t matter but sometimes it does and the error message you get will not really be helpful. For example, calling “openssl req -new –nodes . . .“ will work but calling “openssl req –nodes –new . . . ” will not work and fail with an error message about unrecognized option “-nodes”. While logically this could be explained it’s not really helpful if you are not used to the idiosyncrasies of openssl. While we could use the default “/etc/ssl” as our working directory we do not recommend this. Instead we create a pristine directory with our own setup so we won’t disturb anything else. Later on it is also easy to create a safety backup of this directory. We will therefore create a new directory which we will use to hold all keys and intermediate files. Since openssl keeps track of all certificates we have signed by means of a simple textual database (and a serial number) we must also setup those initial helper files.
In this directory we will have four additional subdirectories:

listitem.para: “private” , Stores all private keys we create
“public”, Stores all public keys (signed certificates)
“csr” , Stores all certificate signing requests (public keys which have not yet been signed)
“newcerts”, Stores a copy all our signed certificates (the “openssl ca” command will automatically store a copy of all signed certificate in this directory).

sect1.para: Start by creating this directory structure as (we will name our root directory “ca”):
sect1.screen: $> mkdir ca $> cd ca $> mkdir private $> mkdir public $> mkdir csr $> mkdir newcerts
sect1.para: Now we create an empty file which later on will hod the the simple text database which “openssl ca” uses to keep track of all certificates that we sign (openssl will complain if this file doesn’t exist).

We shall now create a config file for openssl. One way to do this would be to take the supplied standard openssl config file (in /etc/ssl) and modify a few lines. However, we will create our own smaller version so that we now the exact meaning of every single line we have in the config file. This config file will also have some useful defaults to save us some typing each time we create (or sign) a certificate. We will therefore create our own minimal “our_openssl.cnf” as follows (you should probably name this file after your site and remember to use that name in the commands that follows for clarity).
sect1.programlisting:
#====================================================================== # Simplified openssl config file based on distributed openssl file # Version 1.0 #======================================================================

# In our case we will not really be using Certificate Revocation Lists # but we include the setup for future use crldir = $dir/crl crlnumber = $dir/crlnumber crl = $crldir/crl.pem

sect1.title: Generating the CA key-pair
sect1.para: We are now in position to generate our root (CA) certificate. The first step is to create the key-pair and the signing request
The next step is for us to sign it our self
sect1.screen: $> openssl ca -create_serial -out public/ca_public.pem -selfsign -extensions v3_ca \ -config our_openssl.cnf -days 7000 -infiles csr/ca_public_req.pem
sect1.para: This will prompt you for a number of things most of them have default values as specified in the config file. Do not forget the password you gave here for the CA private key.
The special options used for the CA signing as compared to all the signings we will do from here on are he two options

listitem.para: -selfsign, Which tells openssl to use the ca_public_req.pem when signing instead of expecting a CA certificate (which we haven’t created yet)
-extension v3_ca, needed to read the v3_ca section in the config file.

sect1.para: Our CA certificate (root certificate) will be valid for roughly 20 years (~7000 days). We have now produced the following files:

listitem.para: private/ca_private.pem, The password protected private key part of our CA-key pair. This file should be kept secret at all times!
public/ca_public.pem, The public key that should be imported into browsers that we want to accept any other public leys (certificates) that we will sign in the future.
csr/ca_public_req.pem, The signing request for our CA
serial, This is an administrative file used by “openssl ca” to give a unique serial number for each of the certificate that we sign.

newcerts/<random_serial_number>.pem, A copy of our signed certificate. The exact name is random since it starts with the serial number that was randomly generated. From this moment on each serial number will be incremented by one for each new certificate that we sign.

sect1.para: Many other tutorials show what seems to be a simpler way to create root certificate in only one step using the –x509 option with openssl. As in

listitem.para: You cannot use –create_serial with the “req” command
The signing request is not kept
There is no copy for our signed root certificate in newcerts as it is with all other cert we created

sect1.para: This could however be used in another way. If you need to quickly create a “test-certificate” (which isn’t signed by any trusted authority or yourself) you could create such a certificate in the same way (no need to include the –extensions v3_ca in this case though) such as
You can now use the resulting certificate if you need to run some quick test with some software that requires a SSL/TLS certificate (key-pair).

note.para: Note on x509v3 compliancy. The CA certificate we have created here is, while perfectly working, not formally fully compliant with the very latest version of the PKIX and X509v3 standards since that requires the email address to be specified in a slightly different place. This is however of no practical concern for us (unless you plan on starting your own worldwide certification agency and charge money for signing certificates)

sect1.title: Generating the Apache HTTPS key-pair
sect1.para: We will now generate the key-pair that will allow HTTPS traffic. We will show two ways of doing this. The first (and simplest) is top just generate a key-pair which is valid for exactly one common name, i.e. the name you access the browser with. On a home network where you probably don’t have a DNS server you will most likely access the server via an IP address directly. The problem with only having one name in the certificate is that if you access the browser through some other methods (perhaps from outside your router with a completely different IP address) you might again get a warning about untrusted site even if you have imported browser public key.

The following command will generate a key-pair. As you can see we have added the suffix “_req” to the public key. That is to remind ourself that this will just be used as a certificate signing request, i.e. this public key has not yet been signed by our CA key-pari created in the previous step. After we have signed the key it will be named “https_public.pem”

Answer all the questions that you are now presented with. Keep in mind that every certificate must have a unique distinguished name that is made up of the fields like company name, city, department/unit etc. A recommendation is therefore to use “Web” (or Apache or similar) as the unit name to differentiate this certificate from the other mail certificate we need to create as a next step.

sect1.title: Converting to other certificate formats
sect1.para: As mentioned previously there are other variant formats besides PEM used to store certificates and keys. More specifically there are two other formats commonly usedas described below.

sect2.title: DER format
sect2.para: DER stands for Distinguished Encoding Rules. This format is also quite often used on MS Windows system as well as with Java. This is a binary format so it cannot directly be viewed as a text file (in opposite from the pem format).
Convert an existing certificate in PEM format to the equivalent DER format is straight forward using openssl
sect2.screen: $> openssl x509 -inform pem -in certificate.pem -outform der \ -out certificate.der

sect2.title: PKCS #12 format
sect2.para: PKCS stands for Public-Key Cryptography Standards and #12 is a format in which both a private and a public key is stored in the same file for the purpose of authentication.

The PKCS format is part of a larger set of standards defined by the RSA Laboratories. Some of these standard are also defined as RFCs. This specific standard (#12) is a format used to store client certificates. Client certificates are used in analogy to server certificates but to identify the client and not a server. A server can for example be setup in such a way that a client must have a trusted certificate in order to connect to the server. The server trusts a specific certificate if the certificate have been signed by an authority accepted by the server.
It would bring to far to go through all the details of this format here. However this type of format is handled by the pkcs12 subcommand to openssl command.
To create a client certificate to be used for authentication based on a existing key-pair use the command
One difference here is that the client certificate will be protected by a password so this will have to be given when the certificate is created (openssl will ask for it).
In order to view some details an existing client certificate use the following command
sect2.screen: $> openssl pkcs12 -noout -info -in myclcert.p12 Enter Import Password: <SECRET_PASSWORD> MAC Iteration 2048 MAC verified OK PKCS7 Encrypted data: pbeWithSHA1And40BitRC2-CBC, Iteration 2048 Certificate bag PKCS7 Data Shrouded Keybag: pbeWithSHA1And3-KeyTripleDES-CBC, Iteration 2048
sect2.para: In the output there is a statements about "MAC verified OK". In this context MAC stands for Message Authentication Code and is a way to guarantee that the certificate is valid and has not been tampered with. The reference to PKCS #7 refers to specific message syntax which is detailed in RFC2315

sect1.title: Certification Revocation List (CRL) and OCSP
sect1.para: One thing that we haven't yet touched upon is the directory crl/ under the apache configuration directory. This directory is used to store a Certificate Revocation List. Basically a list of certificates that the issuer might revoked and should no longer be trusted. From the server perspective this is used to verify that any certificate a client might present is still valid.

The problem with such a revocation list is that it must be constantly renewed to be of any value. In addition both the client and the server needs to have access to an updated revocation lists since neither part can really trust the other part.

For the reason with the need of constant updates of the revocation lists this has too large extent been replaced by online direct checking using what is known as OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol). Basically the client will verify any certificate given by the server by going online and check a central revocation lists on a dedicated certificate server.

Ideally all official root certificates (CA certificates) will have ps59D7005DKsuch a server. So for example if a server claims to have a certificate verified by, say, Verisign the client will go online to the Verisign OCSP server and double check that the certificate is really still valid.

We will not discuss this any further in this tutorial but should the need to setup a certificate server arise the open source server "OpenCA" (http://www.openca.org/\) server might be good candidate to examine since it also includes a OCSPD server daemon.

sect1.title: Summary
sect1.para: With the above steps we have created the key-pairs we need for both the Web-server as well as the mail servers (Dovecot2 and postfix). You should now take a backup of this directory and keep it in a safe place. When you later on upgrade your servers you should restore these certificates to avoid client warnings.

Since there is quite a lot of text in the previous section we just repeat the actual commands below that we used to create the key-pairs to make it clearer that it is not that difficult. Each command set first creates the key-pair and then signs it.

caution.para: Remember to uncomment and set the “subjectAltName” in the configuration file if you want your certificates to be valid for multi-homed servers, i.e. servers that are accessed with several different DNS names (but only one IP-address).

sect2.title: Creating the CA (root certificate)
sect2.screen: $> openssl req -new -keyout private/ca_private.pem \ -out csr/ca_public_req.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf $> openssl ca -create_serial -out public/ca_public.pem \ -selfsign -extensions v3_ca -config our_openssl.cnf \ -days 7000 -infiles csr/ca_public_req.pem

sect2.title: Creating the Apache HTTPS certificate
sect2.screen: $> openssl req -new -nodes -keyout private/https_private.pem \ -out csr/https_public_req.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf $> openssl ca -out public/https_public.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf \ -infiles csr/https_public_req.pem

sect2.title: Creating the mail certificate
sect2.screen: $> openssl req -new -nodes -keyout private/mail_private.pem \ -out csr/mail_public_req.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf $> openssl ca -out public/mail_public.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf \ -infiles csr/mail_public_req.pem

appendix.title: Apache virtual host example configuration
appendix.para: The following example configuration shows a complete virtual host configuration for a HTTPS server. The configuration assumes that the host is at IP address 192.168.0.50. You should also notice that this setup relaxes the overly restrictive default settings to allow symbolic links and CGI programs to be executed.
Remember also that in addition to the virtual host configuration file the /etc/sysconfig/apache2 configuration also needs to be updated as described in a previous chapter to allow HTTPS traffic.

sect1.title: ssl-vhost.conf
sect1.para: The following shows an example of a complete virtual host configuration

note.para: The initial <VirtualHost _default_:443> will make these settings apply on all IP addresses that no other virtual host is bound to. Please observe that this is quite different from <VirtualHost *:443> which will match all IP addresses regardless if they are used by other virtual host or not.
The matching is valid only for numeric IP add not DNS names.

sect1.programlisting:
<VirtualHost _default_:443>
# General setup for the virtual host DocumentRoot "/srv/www/vhosts/ssl-htdocs" ServerName 192.168.0.50:443 ServerAdmin root@localhost ErrorLog /var/log/apache2/ssl-htdocs.err TransferLog /var/log/apache2/ssl-htdocs.access CustomLog /var/log/apache2/ssl-htdocs.info ssl_combined
DirectoryIndex index.html
RewriteEngine On RewriteOptions Inherit
HostnameLookups Off UseCanonicalName Off
ServerSignature On
Include /etc/apache2/conf.d/*.conf
<Directory /srv/www/vhosts/ssl-htdocs> AllowOverride All Options Indexes FollowSymLinks ExecCGI Order allow,deny Allow from all </Directory>
ScriptAlias /cgi-bin/ /srv/www/vhosts/ssl-cgi-bin <Directory /srv/www/vhosts/ssl-cgi-bin> AllowOverride All Options +ExecCGI -Includes Order allow,deny Allow from all </Directory>
SSLCertificateFile /etc/apache2/ssl.crt/server.crt SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/apache2/ssl.key/server.key SSLEngine on SSLProtocol all -SSLv2 -SSLv3 SSLCipherSuite ALL:!aNULL:!eNULL:!SSLv2:!LOW:!EXP:!MD5:@STRENGTH
<Files ~ "\.(cgi|shtml|phtml|php3?)$"> SSLOptions +StdEnvVars </Files> <Directory "/srv/www/cgi-bin"> SSLOptions +StdEnvVars </Directory>
SetEnvIf User-Agent ".*MSIE [1-5].*" \ nokeepalive ssl-unclean-shutdown \ downgrade-1.0 force-response-1.0
</VirtualHost>
